class/Players.d: The Players service contains Player objects for presently connected clients to a Roblox server. It also contains information about a place's configuration. It can fetch information about players not connected to the server, such as character appearances, friends, and avatar thumbnail.
class/Players.s: A service that contains presently connected `Class.Player` objects.

m.d: Enables or disables the three Players methods (BanAsync(), UnbanAsync(), and GetBanHistoryAsync()) that constitute the ban API. This property cannot be set through developer-facing Luau and must be set in Studio through the Players properties window.
m.s: Enables or disables the three `Class.Players` methods (`Class.Players:BanAsync()|BanAsync()`, `Class.Players:UnbanAsync()|UnbanAsync()`, and `Class.Players:GetBanHistoryAsync()|GetBanHistoryAsync()`) that constitute the ban API. This property cannot be set through developer-facing Luau and must be set in Studio through the Players properties window.

kid.simple: A switch that turns the ban tools (BanAsync, UnbanAsync, GetBanHistoryAsync) on or off. Scripts can't change it. You tick it in Studio in the Players Properties window.

m.d:
This property indicates whether or not bubble chat is enabled. It is set with the Players:SetChatStyle() method using the ChatStyle enum.

When this chat mode is enabled, the experience displays chats in the chat user interface at the top-left corner of the screen.

There are two other chat modes, Players.ClassicChat and a chat mode where both classic and bubble chat are enabled.
m.s: Indicates whether or not bubble chat is enabled. It is set with the `Class.Players:SetChatStyle()` method.

kid.simple: Read-only true/false that tells you if the old bubble chat style is on. It is set by an internal method scripts can't call, so you will rarely need it.

m.d:
This property indicates whether characters will respawn automatically. The default value is true.

If this property is disabled (false), player characters will not spawn until the Player:LoadCharacterAsync() function is called for each Player, including when players join the experience.

This can be useful in experiences where players have finite lives, such as competitive experiences in which players do not respawn until a round ends.
m.s: Indicates whether `Class.Player.Character|characters` will respawn automatically.

kid.simple: If true (the default), players get a body automatically when they join and after they die. Set it to false if you want to decide yourself when people spawn, for example only at the start of each round.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
Players.CharacterAutoLoads = false -- nobody spawns on their own now

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    task.wait(3) -- wait 3 seconds, like a short lobby countdown
    player:LoadCharacterAsync() -- now spawn them by hand
end)
kid.gotcha: With this off, StarterGui also won't copy into PlayerGui until you call LoadCharacterAsync, so the player sees no custom UI.

m.d:
Indicates whether or not classic chat is enabled. This property is set by the Players:SetChatStyle() method using the ChatStyle enum.

When this chat mode is enabled, the experience displays chats in a bubble above the sender's head.

There are two other chat modes, Players.BubbleChat and a chat mode where both classic and bubble chat are enabled.
m.s: Indicates whether or not classic chat is enabled; set by the `Class.Players:SetChatStyle()` method.

kid.simple: Read-only true/false that tells you if the old classic chat style is on. Set internally, rarely needed.

m.d:
This read-only property refers to the Player whose client is running the experience.

This property is only defined for LocalScripts and ModuleScripts required by them, since they run on the client. For the server, on which Script objects run their code, this property is nil.
m.s: The `Class.Player` that the `Class.LocalScript` is running for.

kid.simple: The Player object of the person on this device. Only works in LocalScripts (code running on the player's own device). On the server it is nil, because the server isn't any one player.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local player = Players.LocalPlayer
print("Hi, " .. player.DisplayName .. "!")
kid.gotcha: Using Players.LocalPlayer in a server Script gives nil and then errors when you try to use it.

m.dep: This property is a deprecated variant of Players.LocalPlayer which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use Players.LocalPlayer instead.

m.d: This property determines the maximum number of players that can be in a server. This property can only be set through a specific place's settings on the Creator Dashboard.
m.s: The maximum number of players that can be in a server.

kid.simple: Read-only number: the most people allowed in one server. You set it in your place settings on the Creator Dashboard, not in a script.
kid.example:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
print("Server holds up to " .. Players.MaxPlayers .. " players")

m.d: This property indicates the number of people in the server at the current time. It is read only. Meaning it cannot be written to, only read.
m.s: Returns the number of people in the server at the current time.
m.dep: This item is deprecated. Instead, of using this item, you should count the number of players returned by Players:GetPlayers().

kid.simple: Old — use #Players:GetPlayers() instead.

m.d: This property indicates the number of people in the server at the current time. It is read only. Meaning it cannot be written to, only read.
m.s: Returns the number of people in the server at the current time.
m.dep: This property is a deprecated variant of Players.NumPlayers which has also been deprecated. Neither property should be used in new work. Instead, you should count the number of players returned by Players:GetPlayers().

kid.simple: Old — use #Players:GetPlayers() instead.

m.d: This property indicates the number of players to which Roblox's matchmaker will fill servers. This number will be less than the maximum number of players (Players.MaxPlayers) supported by the experience.
m.s: The preferred number of players for a server.

kid.simple: Read-only number: how many players Roblox tries to fill a server up to before it starts a new one. It is less than MaxPlayers so friends still have room to join.

m.d:
This property controls the time, in seconds, it takes for a player to respawn when Players.CharacterAutoLoads is true. It defaults to 5.0 seconds.

This is useful when you want to change how long it takes to respawn based on the type of your experience but don't want to handle spawning players individually.

Although this property can be set from within a Script, you can more easily set it directly on the Players object in Studio's Explorer window.
m.s: Controls the amount of time taken for a players character to respawn.

kid.simple: How many seconds a player waits after dying before a new body appears. The default is 5. Only matters when CharacterAutoLoads is true.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
Players.RespawnTime = 1 -- fast respawns for an obby

m.d:
When enabled, R15 character Humanoids play directional locomotion animations, strafing sideways and backpedaling while keeping their current facing direction instead of rotating to face whichever direction they move. When disabled, characters turn to face their direction of movement. Defaults to false.

This property cannot be set through developer-facing Luau and must be set in Studio through the Players properties window.
m.s: Determines whether R15 character models play directional strafing and backpedaling animations instead of always turning to face their direction of movement.

kid.simple: A Studio-only setting (scripts can't change it). When on, R15 characters can walk sideways and backwards while still facing forward, instead of always turning to face where they walk. Default is off.

m.d:
The Players:BanAsync() method allows you to easily ban users who violate your experience's guidelines. You can specify the ban duration, enable the ban to propagate to suspected alternate accounts, enable the ban to temporarily block the banned user's device from rejoining the experience, and provide a message to the banned user in accordance with the Usage Guidelines. You should also post your experience rules somewhere accessible to all users and provide a way for them to appeal. This method is enabled and disabled by the Players.BanningEnabled property, which you can toggle in Studio.

Banning and Messaging

Banned users will be immediately evicted and prevented from rejoining your experiences. They will be presented with an error modal displaying the time left on their ban and your DisplayReason. Roblox's backend systems will evict players across all servers from the place(s) that you specify. DisplayReason can have a maximum length of 400 characters and is subject to a text filter. For more information on acceptable modal text, see ban messaging.

Places and Universe

By default, bans extend to any place within that universe. To limit the ban to only the place from which this API is called, configure ApplyToUniverse to false. However, if a user is banned in the start place of the universe, it effectively results in the user being excluded from the entirety of the universe, irrespective of whether a universal ban is in place or not.

Alternative Accounts

Users often play under multiple different accounts, known as alternate accounts, which are sometimes used to circumvent account bans. To help you keep banned users out, the default behavior of this API will propagate all bans from the source account you banned to any of their suspected alternate accounts. You can turn off ban propagations to alternate accounts by configuring ExcludeAltAccounts to true.

Device Blocks

To help address disruptive users who circumvent alternate account detection, set ApplyDeviceBlock to true. This blocks the banned user's device from rejoining the experience for 24 hours after the ban is applied.

Ban Duration

Not all transgressions are the same, so not all bans should be the same length. This API lets you configure the duration of the ban, in seconds, with the Duration field. To specify a permanent ban, set the field to -1. You may also want to dynamically configure the ban duration based on the user's ban history, which you can query for using Players:GetBanHistoryAsync(). For example, you may want to consider the number of bans, the duration of previous bans, or build logic off of the notes you save under PrivateReason which can be up to 1000 characters and are not text filtered. PrivateReason notes are never shared with the client and can be considered safe from attackers.

Errors and Throttling

This method invokes an HTTP call to backend services which are subject to throttling and may fail. If you're calling this API with more than one UserId, this method will attempt to make the HTTP call for each ID. It will then aggregate any error messages and join them as a comma separated list. For example, if this method is invoked for five users and requests for those with UserIds 2 and 4 fail, the following error message appears:

HTTP failure for UserId 2: Timedout, HTTP 504 (Service unavailable) failure for UserId 4: Service exception

The message will always include failure for UserId {} if it is an HTTP error.

Client-Side Requirement

Because of the risks associated with banning users, this method may only be called on the backend experience server (client-side calls will result in an error). You may test this API in Studio, during collaborative creation, or in a team test, but the bans will not apply to production.

This API uses the User Restrictions Open Cloud API. You will be able to utilize these APIs to manage your bans in third party applications.
m.s: Bans users from your experience, with options to specify duration, reason, whether the ban applies to the entire universe or just the current place, and more. This method is enabled and disabled by the `Class.Players.BanningEnabled` property, which you can toggle in Studio.

p.s:
• UserIds (required; array) — Array of UserIds of players to be banned. Max size is 50.

  • ApplyToUniverse (optional; boolean) — Whether ban propagates to all places within the experience universe. Default is true.

  • Duration (required; integer) — Duration of the ban, in seconds. Permanent bans should have a value of -1. 0 and all other negative values are invalid.

  • DisplayReason (required; string) — The message that will be displayed to users when they attempt to and fail to join an experience. Maximum string length is 400.

  • PrivateReason (required; string) — Internal messaging that will be returned when querying the user's ban history. Maximum string length is 1000.

  • ExcludeAltAccounts (optional; boolean) — When true, Roblox does not attempt to ban alternate accounts. Default is false.

  • ApplyDeviceBlock (optional; boolean) — When true, Roblox will block banned users' devices from rejoining the experience for 24 hours after the ban is applied. Default is false. The block can be overridden by unbanning a user via a call to Players:UnbanAsync(). Note that unbanning a user through any other method will not lift the device block.

kid.simple: Bans one or more users from your game for a set time or forever. You give it a table with who, how long (in seconds, -1 means forever), a message they see, and a private note for yourself. It can also ban their alt accounts and block their device for 24 hours.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService (turn on BanningEnabled in Studio first)
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local ok, err = pcall(function()
    Players:BanAsync({
        UserIds = { 123456789 },          -- the UserId(s) to ban
        Duration = 3600,                  -- 3600 seconds = 1 hour
        DisplayReason = "Please follow the rules.", -- they see this
        PrivateReason = "Spamming chat",  -- only you see this
        ApplyDeviceBlock = true,          -- also block their computer for 24 hours
    })
end)
if not ok then
    warn(err)
end
kid.gotcha: Server only, needs BanningEnabled, and bans made while testing in Studio don't apply to the real game. Device blocks only work on Windows and macOS.

m.d:
This function returns information about a player's avatar on the Roblox website in the form of a dictionary. It is not to be confused with GetCharacterAppearanceAsync, which actually loads the assets described by this method. You can use InsertService:LoadAsset() to load the assets that are used in the player's avatar. The structure of the returned dictionary is as follows:

Name Type Description
assets table (see below) Describes the equipped assets (hats, body parts, etc)
bodyColors table (see below) Describes the BrickColor values for each limb
bodyColor3s table (see below) Describes the Color3 instance for each limb which may not match perfectly with bodyColors
defaultPantsApplied bool Describes whether default pants are applied
defaultShirtApplied bool Describes whether default shirt is applied
emotes table (see below) Describes the equipped emote animations
playerAvatarType string Either "R15" or "R6"
scales table (see below) Describes various body scaling factors

Assets Sub-Table

The assets table is an array of tables containing the following keys that describe the assets currently equipped by the player:

Name Type Description
id number The asset ID of the equipped asset
assetType table A table with name and id fields, each describing the kind of asset equipped ("Hat", "Face", etc.)
name string The name of the equipped asset

Scales Sub-Table

The scales table has the following keys, each a number corresponding to one Humanoid scaling property: bodyType, head, height, proportion, depth, width.

Body Colors Sub-Table

The bodyColors table has the following keys, each a number corresponding to a BrickColor ID number which can be used with BrickColor.new(id): leftArmColorId, torsoColorId, rightArmColorId, headColorId, leftLegColorId, rightLegColorId.
m.s: Returns information about the character appearance of a given user.

p.s: The *userId of the specified player.

r.s: A dictionary containing information about the character appearance of a given user.

m.d:
Unbans players banned from Players:BanAsync() or the User Restrictions Open Cloud API. This method is enabled and disabled by the Players.BanningEnabled property, which you can toggle in Studio.

Like Players:BanAsync(), this method takes in a config dictionary that will let you bulk unban users. This configures the users that are unbanned and the scope from which they are unbanned from.

Unbans will only take effect on bans with the same ApplyToUniverse scope. For example, an unban with ApplyToUniverse set to true will not invalidate a previous ban with ApplyToUniverse set to false. In other words, a universe level unban will not invalidate a place level ban. The opposite also holds true.

For the case where a user's device may be blocked by a ban where ApplyDeviceBlock was set to true, an unban applied by this method will override the device block for the unbanned player. Please note that unbanning a user through any other method, such as the Open Cloud API or the Creator Hub, will not lift the device block.

This method invokes a HTTP call to backend services, which are throttled and may fail. If you are calling this API with multiple UserIds, this method will attempt to make this HTTP call for each UserId. It will then aggregate any error messages and join them as a comma separated list. For example, if this method is invoked for five UserIds: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and requests for users 2 and 4 fail then the following error message appears: HTTP failure for UserId 2: Timedout, HTTP 504 (Service unavailable) failure for UserId 4: Service exception. The message will always include failure for UserId {} if it is an HTTP error. It is undefined behavior if you pass in both valid and invalid UserIds, i.e. a UserId that is not a positive number, as some network requests may succeed before all input is validated.

Because of the risks associated with banning users, this method may only be called on the backend server. Client side calls will result in an error. You may test this API in Studio, Team Create, and Team Test, but the bans will not apply to production. This function call will only attempt ban requests on production servers and not in Studio testing. However, all input validation steps will still work in Studio.

This API uses the User Restrictions Open Cloud API. You will be able to utilize these APIs to manage your bans in third party applications.

kid.simple: Lets banned users back into your game. Give it a table with UserIds and ApplyToUniverse. It also lifts any device block made by BanAsync.

-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ok, err = pcall(function()
    Players:UnbanAsync({
        UserIds = { 123456789 },
        ApplyToUniverse = true, -- must match the ban's setting
    })
end)
if not ok then
    warn(err)
end

This can be used alongside the Players.PlayerRemoving event, which fires when a player is about to leave the experience. For instance, if you would like print a message every time a new player joins or leaves:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    print(player.Name .. " joined the experience!")
end)

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player, reason)
    print(player.Name .. " left the experience! Reason: " .. tostring(exitReason))
end)

If you want to track when a player's character is added or removed from the experience, such as when a player respawns or dies, you can use the Player.CharacterAdded and Player.CharacterRemoving functions.

Note that this event does not work as expected in a solo playtest mode because the player is created before scripts run that connect to PlayerAdded. To handle this case, as well as cases in which the script is added into the experience after a player enters, create an onPlayerAdded() function that you can call to handle a player's entrance.

kid.simple: Fires once each time a person joins the server, and hands you their Player object. The usual place to load data, make a leaderboard, or put them on a team.

-- Script in ServerScriptService
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local function onPlayerAdded(player)
    print("Welcome, " .. player.DisplayName)
end

for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
    onPlayerAdded(player) -- people already here
end
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded) -- people who join later

kid.simple: Players is the service that keeps track of everyone who is in your game server right now. Every person who joins gets a Player object placed inside it, and that object is taken out when they leave. It also has the events that tell your scripts when someone joins or leaves, plus tools for looking up users, building avatars, and banning rule-breakers.
kid.analogy: Players is like the front desk of a hotel. It has the guest book (who is staying right now), it rings a bell when a guest checks in (PlayerAdded) and when one checks out (PlayerRemoving), and it can look up any guest's name or ID card. It can even put someone on the 'not allowed back' list (BanAsync).
whenToUse: Run code when a player joins or leaves (give them stats, load or save their data).
Loop over everyone in the server, for example to start a round or give everyone a prize.
Find which player owns a character that touched something (GetPlayerFromCharacter).
Get the player who is running a LocalScript (Players.LocalPlayer).
Change how long it takes to respawn (RespawnTime) or stop automatic spawning (CharacterAutoLoads).
Ban or unban users who break your game's rules (BanAsync, UnbanAsync).
kid.where: Server and client. It is a service, so you get it with `local Players = game:GetService("Players")`. You can see it in the Explorer window. Some things only work on one side: LocalPlayer only works on the client, and the ban methods only work on the server.

terms.service: A special built-in object that does one big job for the whole game. You get services with game:GetService("Name").
terms.Player: The object that stands for one real person connected to your game. It is not their body. The body is the Character.
terms.Character: The 3D body (a Model with a Humanoid inside) that a player walks around with. It is created when they spawn and removed when they die and respawn.
terms.client: The player's own device (computer, phone, console). LocalScripts run there.
terms.server: The Roblox computer that runs the game for everyone in that server. Normal Scripts run there. It is the boss that everyone trusts.
terms.event: Something that happens in the game, like a player joining. You can :Connect a function to an event so your function runs every time it happens.
terms.Connect: How you tell an event 'run this function when you happen'.
terms.nil: Luau's word for 'nothing' or 'no value'. If a lookup finds nobody, you get nil.
terms.UserId: A number that belongs to one Roblox account and never changes, even if the user changes their name. Best way to save data for a player.
terms.yield: When a function makes your script pause and wait (for example while it asks the Roblox website something). Functions ending in Async usually yield.
terms.Async: Short for asynchronous. A function that has to wait for something (often the internet) before it can give an answer, so it pauses your script.
terms.pcall: Short for protected call. It runs a function and catches errors instead of letting them crash your script. Use it around things that talk to the internet.
terms.respawn: Coming back to life with a new character after dying.
terms.ban: Blocking a user from joining your game, for a set time or forever.
terms.alt account: A second (alternate) account someone makes, sometimes to sneak back in after a ban.
terms.device block: An extra ban option that blocks the computer itself from rejoining for 24 hours, so the person can't just log in on another account on the same computer.
terms.universe: Your whole game (sometimes called an experience), including every place inside it. A ban can cover the whole universe or just one place.
terms.dictionary: A table where each value has a name (a key), like { Duration = 60, DisplayReason = "Cheating" }.
terms.plugin: A tool that runs inside Roblox Studio to help you build. Some methods are only allowed for plugins, not your game scripts.
terms.HumanoidDescription: An object that lists everything about an avatar's look: hats, clothes, body colors, sizes, animations.
terms.thumbnail: A small picture, like a headshot of someone's avatar.

examples.title: The full player lifecycle: join, spawn, die, respawn, leave
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

-- How many seconds a dead player waits before coming back (default is 5)
Players.RespawnTime = 3

local function onCharacterAdded(character)
    -- Step 2: the player's body has spawned (this happens again after every respawn)
    local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
    print(player.Name .. " spawned")

    local humanoid = character:WaitForChild("Humanoid")
    humanoid.Died:Connect(function()
        -- Step 3: the body died. After RespawnTime seconds Roblox removes it
        print(player.Name .. " died, respawning in " .. Players.RespawnTime .. " seconds")
    end)
end

local function onCharacterRemoving(character)
    -- Step 4: the old body is about to be removed (right before a respawn, or when leaving)
    print("Removing old body: " .. character.Name)
end

local function onPlayerAdded(player)
    -- Step 1: a person joined the server
    print(player.Name .. " joined! UserId: " .. player.UserId)

    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(onCharacterAdded)
    player.CharacterRemoving:Connect(onCharacterRemoving)

    -- If the character already exists (can happen in Studio), handle it now
    if player.Character then
        onCharacterAdded(player.Character)
    end
end

local function onPlayerRemoving(player)
    -- Step 5: the person is leaving. The Player object still exists right now,
    -- so this is the place to save their data.
    print(player.Name .. " is leaving")
end

-- Handle anyone who joined before this script started (common in Studio Play tests)
for _, player in Players:GetPlayers() do
    task.spawn(onPlayerAdded, player)
end
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(onPlayerAdded)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(onPlayerRemoving)
explain: The order things happen in is always: PlayerAdded (joined) -> CharacterAdded (body spawned) -> Humanoid.Died (body died) -> wait RespawnTime seconds -> CharacterRemoving (old body removed) -> CharacterAdded again (new body) -> ... -> PlayerRemoving (left the game).
PlayerAdded and PlayerRemoving happen once per visit. CharacterAdded and CharacterRemoving can happen many times, once for every life.
We connect CharacterAdded inside onPlayerAdded, because each player has their own CharacterAdded event.
We also call onCharacterAdded right away if player.Character already exists, in case the body spawned before we connected.

The loop over Players:GetPlayers() catches anyone who was already in the game before the script connected to PlayerAdded. In Studio solo tests your player is often created before scripts run, so without this loop PlayerAdded might never fire for you.
task.spawn runs onPlayerAdded for each player without waiting for one to finish before starting the next.

examples.title: Where things get copied when a player joins and spawns
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    -- These four containers live inside every Player object:
    --   Backpack      = their inventory of Tools. Filled from StarterPack + StarterGear each spawn.
    --   StarterGear   = this player's own personal 'always give me this' Tools.
    --   PlayerGui     = what shows on their screen. Filled from StarterGui on spawn.
    --   PlayerScripts = client scripts from StarterPlayer > StarterPlayerScripts.
    --                   The server can NOT see inside PlayerScripts.
    local backpack = player:WaitForChild("Backpack")
    local starterGear = player:WaitForChild("StarterGear")
    local playerGui = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")
    print(player.Name, backpack, starterGear, playerGui)

    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(character)
        -- By now StarterCharacterScripts have been copied into the character,
        -- and StarterPack tools have been copied into a fresh Backpack.
        print(player.Name .. " has " .. #player.Backpack:GetChildren() .. " tools")
    end)
end)
explain: The Starter containers you edit in Studio are like templates. When the game runs, Roblox copies them into each player.
StarterGui -> PlayerGui: copied when the character spawns.
StarterPack -> Backpack: copied every time the character spawns. When the character dies, the old Backpack is thrown away and a new one is made.
StarterGear (inside the Player) -> Backpack: also copied every spawn, but it is personal to that one player. A good place to put a tool they bought so they keep it after dying.
StarterPlayer > StarterPlayerScripts -> PlayerScripts: copied once when the player joins. Good for scripts that should keep running even when the character dies, like input controls.
StarterPlayer > StarterCharacterScripts -> inside the Character model: copied every spawn.
WaitForChild waits until the child exists, because these containers might be created a moment after PlayerAdded fires.

examples.title: Ban a cheater (with device block) and unban them later
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (BanningEnabled must be turned on in the Players properties in Studio)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local function banPlayer(player, reasonForPlayer, secretNotes)
    local config = {
        UserIds = { player.UserId },   -- who to ban (up to 50 at once)
        Duration = 60 * 60 * 24,       -- seconds: 1 day. Use -1 for forever
        DisplayReason = reasonForPlayer, -- shown to the banned user (max 400 chars, filtered)
        PrivateReason = secretNotes,   -- only you see this, in ban history (max 1000 chars)
        ExcludeAltAccounts = false,    -- false = also ban their suspected alt accounts
        ApplyToUniverse = true,        -- true = banned from every place in this game
        ApplyDeviceBlock = true,       -- also block their computer for 24 hours
    }

    -- BanAsync talks to Roblox's servers, so it can fail. pcall catches the error.
    local ok, err = pcall(function()
        Players:BanAsync(config)
    end)
    if not ok then
        warn("Ban failed: " .. tostring(err))
    end
end

local function unbanUser(userId)
    local ok, err = pcall(function()
        Players:UnbanAsync({
            UserIds = { userId },
            ApplyToUniverse = true, -- must match how the ban was made
        })
    end)
    if not ok then
        warn("Unban failed: " .. tostring(err))
    end
end

-- Example: someone fired a suspicious remote. (Your own cheat check goes here.)
-- banPlayer(somePlayer, "Exploiting is against the rules. Appeal on our group page.", "Teleported 500 studs in 0.1s")
explain: BanAsync takes one table (a dictionary) that describes the ban. UserIds, Duration, DisplayReason and PrivateReason are required.
Duration is in seconds. 3600 is one hour, 86400 is one day, and -1 means a permanent ban. 0 or other negative numbers are not allowed.
DisplayReason is what the banned person sees on their error screen. It goes through Roblox's text filter. You may mention places like 'our Discord' but not usernames or direct links.
PrivateReason is a note for you and your team. It is never sent to players, and you can read it later with GetBanHistoryAsync.
By default bans also reach the person's suspected alt accounts. Set ExcludeAltAccounts = true to turn that off.

ApplyDeviceBlock = true also blocks the banned person's device for 24 hours, so they can't hop onto a different account on the same computer. It only works for players currently in your game, only on Windows and macOS (not phones or consoles), and it does not ban the other accounts on that device.
Unbanning with UnbanAsync removes the device block too. Unbanning from the Creator Hub or Open Cloud does NOT remove the device block.
An unban only cancels a ban with the same ApplyToUniverse setting. A whole-game unban won't undo a single-place ban, and the other way around.
Banned players are kicked right away from all servers and see how long is left on their ban.
These methods only work on the server, only when Players.BanningEnabled is on, and bans made while testing in Studio don't affect the real game.
Rules: post your game rules where everyone can see them, apply them fairly to everyone, and let people appeal.

examples.title: Find who touched a part
examples.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local part = script.Parent

part.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
    -- otherPart is the body part that bumped into us, like a LeftFoot
    local character = otherPart.Parent
    local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
    if player then
        print(player.Name .. " touched the part!")
    end
end)
explain: Touched gives you the part that touched, not the player.
The body part's Parent is the character Model.
GetPlayerFromCharacter turns that character into its Player, or gives nil if it was an NPC or a falling brick.

gotchas: PlayerAdded may not fire for you in a Studio solo test, because your player joins before the script connects. Always also loop over Players:GetPlayers() once at the start.
Players.LocalPlayer is nil in a server Script. It only works in LocalScripts (and ModuleScripts they require).
Use player.UserId (or player.User) to save data, not player.Name. Names can change, UserIds never do.
Functions that end in Async talk to the internet and can fail. Wrap them in pcall.
BanAsync, UnbanAsync and GetBanHistoryAsync error unless BanningEnabled is turned on in Studio, and they only run on the server.
Don't let the client decide who gets banned or kicked. A cheater could fire your RemoteEvent with someone else's name. Make the server check everything.

class/PluginCapabilities.d: PluginCapabilities describes what a plugin is allowed to do. Its Manifest property holds a JSON string that declares which data models the plugin targets (such as Edit, Server, and Client) and the permissions the plugin requests. It's used by built-in and standalone plugins to record their declared capabilities.

class/PluginConnection.d:
Studio plugins run in each Studio data model that the user opens, including both edit and playtest data models. PluginConnection objects allow these instances of the same plugin to communicate across data model boundaries. Messages sent by PluginConnection:SendMessage() will be received in the remote data model via the callback the same plugin registers with PluginConnection:BindToMessage(). Each PluginConnection object can both send and receive messages while connected, and messages will be received reliably and in order unless the connection drops (e.g. due to the remote data model shutting down) before their receipt.

Note that although multiple plugins may share the same PluginConnection object, they each have their own internal connection; each plugin will receive only its own messages in its callback to BindToMessage(), even if other plugins call SendMessage().
class/PluginConnection.s: Encapsulates a connection between the current data model and another for plugin communication.

m.d: If true, then this PluginConnection remains connected to the target data model, and it is still possible to send messages to that data model and receive them from it. If false, then the connection has been lost. Once disconnected, PluginConnection objects cannot reconnect, so a value of false here indicates it is now safe to discard the PluginConnection object.
m.s: Whether this `PluginConnection` object is still connected.

m.d: This string contains a globally unique identifier for the target data model, which will be the same for any two plugin connections that target the same data model (even if those connections originate from different data models). This property is immutable.
m.s: A unique ID for the target data model.

m.d: This PluginConnectionTargetType describes the relationship of the target data model to the current data model. For example, a value of PluginConnectionTargetType.Test means that the target data model is a playtest data model spawned from this data model. Alternatively, a value of PluginConnectionTargetType.Edit means the target data model is the edit session which spawned this test data model. This property is immutable.
m.s: This `Enum.PluginConnectionTargetType` describes the relationship of the target data model to the current one.

m.d: This function binds a callback to this connection, which will be called when the connection receives a message from the current plugin running in the remote data model. The message passed to the callback will be the same as the one the plugin passed to SendMessage(). The PluginConnection will buffer any messages received before the plugin calls BindToMessage() and deliver them immediately when the plugin does call BindToMessage(). Each plugin may only bind one callback at a time.
m.s: Binds a callback to this `PluginConnection` to receive messages from `SendMessage()`.

p.s: A function accepting a string or a buffer which will be called when this PluginConnection receives a message.

r.s: A RBXScriptConnection representing the binding of this callback to the PluginConnection. Disconnect it to disconnect this callback from the connection.

m.d: This function transmits a string or buffer to the remote data model. The callback registered in BindToMessage() by the instance of the current plugin running in the remote data model will be called asynchronously with the message as its argument.
m.s: Sends a payload to the remote data model.

p.s: The string or buffer to be sent.

This method binds a function that runs when the user clicks the close button of the PluginGui. The widget closes and its Enabled property becomes false even when a function is bound, so the function can't prevent or delay closing. Use it to perform tasks such as saving work when the widget closes.

For example, the following code saves work when the user closes the widget:

local function saveWork()
    -- Save the user's work here.
end

pluginGui:BindToClose(function()

end)

pluginGui:BindToClose()

class/PluginToolbarButton.d:
A PluginToolbarButton object is created through the PluginToolbar:CreateButton() function. It allows the user to initiate a single, one-off action in Roblox Studio through the Click event. Toolbar buttons can also be assigned a keyboard shortcut through Studio's File ⟩ Customize Shortcuts window.

When pressed, the Click event fires. A button will also remain in the pressed state, which may be set manually using SetActive(). Upon plugin activation (Plugin:Activate()), buttons in all other PluginToolbars will be toggled off. If all buttons in a toolbar are off, the toolbar's plugin is deactivated (Plugin:Deactivate()).

When the game viewport is not visible, buttons will be disabled as if their Enabled property were false. Disabled buttons are desaturated and do not respond to user clicks. By setting ClickableWhenViewportHidden to true, you can allow plugin buttons to remain clickable, such as during script editing.
class/PluginToolbarButton.s: A button on a `Class.PluginToolbar` in the Studio ribbon, created by `Class.PluginToolbar:CreateButton()`, that fires `Class.PluginToolbarButton.Click|Click` when pressed.

m.d:
This property determines whether a PluginToolbarButton may be clicked while the 3D viewport is hidden, such as when a Script is being edited in another tab.

Typically, this property should be enabled if an action triggered by a plugin button's Click event doesn't occur in the 3D world (Workspace). For example, a button that opens a widget should have this property as true, since showing a widget is visible to the user even if the 3D view isn't visible.
m.s: Determines whether the button can be clicked when the 3D viewport is hidden, such as when a `Class.Script` is being edited in another tab.

m.d:
This property determines whether a button is clickable in general. When false, the button will be greyed out and unclickable, preventing the user from firing the Click event. Buttons are enabled by default.

Name Type Required for Description

ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted Boolean Any experience that has paid random items. When true, the player can not interact with paid random item generators, either via in‑experience currency bought with Robux or Robux directly.

class/Pose.d:
A Pose holds the CFrame applied to the Motor6D connected to its associated BasePart. The part which is controlled depends on the name of the Pose.

Poses are the fundamental building blocks of animations and, with Keyframes, make up KeyframeSequences.

Poses, joints and hierarchy

Although a Pose is assigned to a BasePart by name, the object manipulated during animation playback is actually the Motor6D connected to this part. Animation rigs branch out from the model's root part through such joints.

In an R15 character rig, the root part is the HumanoidRootPart. The LowerTorso is connected to the HumanoidRootPart by the a motor named 'Root'. Therefore, the CFrame of a Pose named 'LowerTorso' in a Keyframe would be applied to the motor named 'Root', and not the LowerTorso itself.

Poses are arranged in a Keyframe based on joint hierarchy. This means, the Pose's CFrame is applied to the motor connecting the part associated with the pose to the part associated with the pose's parent. See below for a visual example of the structure of Poses on a R15 character.

Pose CFrame

The Roblox animation system applies Pose.CFrame to the corresponding Motor6D by manipulating the relative transformation of the motor, the Motor6D.Transform property. The original C0 and C1 values are not changed.

class/PrismaticConstraint.d:
A PrismaticConstraint creates a rigid joint between two Attachments, allowing them to slide along one axis but not rotate. This constrains the attachments so that their X axes are collinear but pointing in opposite directions. It also constrains the attachments so that their Y axes are parallel.

This constraint inherits many properties from SlidingBallConstraint including ActuatorType, LimitsEnabled, Velocity, and more. Please refer to SlidingBallConstraint for details on configuring a PrismaticConstraint.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.
class/PrismaticConstraint.s: Constraint which creates a rigid joint between two `Class.Attachment|Attachments`, allowing them to slide along one axis but not rotate.

kid.simple: PrismaticConstraint lets two parts slide along one straight line but never twist. The attachments' X arrows form the sliding track. You can let it slide freely, power it like a motor, or make it slide to an exact spot like a servo. Most of its settings come from SlidingBallConstraint.
kid.analogy: PrismaticConstraint is like a drawer in a desk or a sliding door: it only moves in and out along one track.
whenToUse: Elevators and lifts
Sliding doors and drawers
Pistons and crushers in an obby
kid.where: Make it with Instance.new("PrismaticConstraint"), set Attachment0 and Attachment1 (one in each part) and put it in workspace. The sliding line is along the attachments' X arrows. Its settings (ActuatorType, TargetPosition, LimitsEnabled...) come from SlidingBallConstraint.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.axis: An imaginary line something turns around or slides along. An attachment's X axis is its main arrow.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.force: A push or pull. In Roblox it is measured in Roblox force units (mass x studs per second per second). A bigger number is a harder push.
terms.actuator: The part of a constraint that powers movement by itself, like a motor. ActuatorType picks None (no power), Motor (keep spinning/moving at a speed) or Servo (move to a target spot and stop).
terms.motor (ActuatorType): Keeps turning or sliding at a set speed, like a fan or a car wheel.
terms.servo (ActuatorType): Moves to a set target angle or position and holds there, like a robot arm or an automatic door.
terms.limits: Stops that keep a joint from moving too far, like a door that can only swing 90 degrees.
terms.restitution: Bounciness, from 0 (no bounce, just stops) to 1 (bounces back as hard as it hit).
terms.stud: Roblox's unit of length. A default baseplate grid square is 1 stud; a classic character is about 5 studs tall.
terms.SlidingBallConstraint: The parent class that PrismaticConstraint gets all its sliding settings from, like Velocity, TargetPosition and LowerLimit.
terms.collinear: Lying on the same straight line. The sliding track is the line along the attachments' X arrows.

examples.title: A simple elevator
examples.code:
local shaft = workspace:WaitForChild("Shaft")       -- anchored
local platform = workspace:WaitForChild("Platform") -- unanchored

-- Point both attachments' X arrows straight up (the sliding track)
local upward = CFrame.Angles(0, 0, math.rad(90))
local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = shaft
a0.WorldCFrame = CFrame.new(platform.Position) * upward
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = platform
a1.WorldCFrame = a0.WorldCFrame

local slider = Instance.new("PrismaticConstraint")
slider.Attachment0 = a0
slider.Attachment1 = a1
slider.ActuatorType = Enum.ActuatorType.Servo
slider.ServoMaxForce = 100000 -- strong enough to lift players
slider.Speed = 8              -- studs per second
slider.TargetPosition = 0     -- start at the bottom
slider.Parent = shaft

while true do
	task.wait(4)
	slider.TargetPosition = 20 -- go up 20 studs
	task.wait(4)
	slider.TargetPosition = 0  -- come back down
end
explain: Rotating the attachments 90 degrees around Z makes their X arrows point up, so the track is vertical.
Servo mode slides to TargetPosition (a distance in studs along the track) and holds there.
Speed controls how fast it slides; ServoMaxForce must beat the weight of the platform plus riders.
The loop sends it up 20 studs and back down every 4 seconds.

gotchas: The track runs along the attachments' X arrows. If it slides sideways, rotate the attachments.
Lifting needs enough force to beat gravity: at least mass x 196.2 for the platform and everything on it.
The sliding settings live on SlidingBallConstraint; look there for full details on each one.

class/ProceduralModel.d:
ProceduralModel inherits from Model and supports edit-time procedural generation of its contents. Instead of manually constructing model content, a procedural model generates its contents automatically in response to parameter changes.

Generation is defined by a generator module, a ModuleScript referenced by the Generator property. The engine invokes the module's OnGenerate function to produce the model's contents.

A procedural model regenerates when any of the following inputs change:

  • The Size property of the procedural model, which defines a bounding box for the model to generate within.
  • Any attributes on the procedural mode, as defined by the generator module.
  • The generator's module sandboxing configuration (Sandboxed and Capabilities).
  • The source code of the generator module.

When any of these inputs change, the engine schedules regeneration. This scheduled regeneration is performed by calling OnGenerate and applying its results once it returns. In most cases, generation happens within the same frame, but can be deferred to maintain performance.
class/ProceduralModel.s: Procedural models support edit-time procedural generation. Instead of manually constructing model content, a procedural model generates its contents automatically in response to parameter changes.

m.d: If the generator module encounters an error during generation, the contents of the ProceduralModel are replaced with an error state placeholder. The error is stored in the GenerationError property to give you visibility into why the generation failed.
m.s: Stores errors that the generator module might encounter during generation.

m.d:
A reference to a ModuleScript containing code that defines how the ProceduralModel generates its contents in response to parameter changes.

Setting Generator triggers generation using the new generator module. The Attributes table exported by the module is automatically applied as default attribute values on the ProceduralModel.

Clearing Generator preserves the current contents of the ProceduralModel, and prevents further generation until a new generator is assigned.

Guidelines for writing the generator module's OnGenerate function:

  • Only write results into the provided targetContainer. OnGenerate should not modify the DataModel directly; writes elsewhere may not interact correctly with engine systems.
  • OnGenerate is allowed to yield and call yielding methods (for example, GeometryService CSG APIs). Generation is considered complete whenever OnGenerate returns.
  • Calling parameters:Pause() inside long-running loops lets the engine break up work. It only yields when needed to avoid dropping frames, so calls are low-cost when the frame budget is not exceeded.
m.s: A reference to a `Class.ModuleScript` that contains code which defines how the `ProceduralModel` generates its contents in response to parameter changes.

m.d:
The Size of a ProceduralModel defines the bounding volume used for generation.

In a standard model, size is a derived output value based on its contents and can be queried using GetBoundingBox(). A procedural model inverts this relationship: Size is an input that determines how generation occurs, and is explicitly set as a property.

The Size property represents the physical dimensions of the ProceduralModel and is affected by ScaleTo. The OnGenerate function in a generator module doesn't need to account for position or scaling: it produces a result of the specified Size around the origin at a scale of 1, and the procedural model system automatically uses PivotTo() and ScaleTo() to place and scale the output in the ProceduralModel.
m.s: Defines the bounding volume used for generation.

m.d:
Generation is normally scheduled soon after a parameter changes so work can be deferred for performance. ForceGeneration() instead runs any pending generation synchronously and returns whether the ProceduralModel is up to date.

If nothing is pending, returns true without regenerating. Otherwise runs the generator to completion under a hard timeout, then returns true only if the model is no longer waiting to regenerate and produced no GenerationError. On failure or timeout, returns false and re-queues normal scheduled generation. Unlike scheduled generation, a forced generation doesn't yield to preserve the frame budget, so parameters:Pause() inside the generator returns without pausing.

Throws if called from within a generator's OnGenerate function.
m.s: Immediately runs any pending generation instead of waiting for the scheduled regeneration.

r.s: Whether the ProceduralModel is up to date after the call: true if generation completed successfully or nothing needed to be regenerated, false otherwise.

m.d:
Generation is scheduled to run as soon as possible after a parameter changes, but not immediately. Use WaitForGenerationAsync() to wait for generation to complete before parameters are changed.

This method errors if called on a ProceduralModel that is not in the DataModel because generation isn't performed for instances without a parent.

This method returns false if the ProceduralModel is removed from the DataModel while generation is in progress, since this cancels the operation.
m.s: Waits for generation to complete after making parameter changes.

class/ProximityPrompt.d:
The ProximityPrompt instance lets you prompt players to interact with an object in the 3D world, such as opening a door or picking up an item. A ProximityPrompt object works when parented to a BasePart, Attachment, or Model (with PrimaryPart set) in the workspace. When the player's character approaches, a UI appears to prompt them for input.

Prompts consist of three primary elements, each of which can be controlled by the noted properties. The default UI can be swapped out for your own custom appearance as outlined in Style.

Property Description Default
Class.ProximityPrompt.ObjectText|ObjectText An optional name for the object being interacted with.
Class.ProximityPrompt.ActionText|ActionText An optional action name shown to the player. Interact
Class.ProximityPrompt.KeyboardKeyCode|KeyboardKeyCode The keyboard key which will trigger the prompt. E
Class.ProximityPrompt.GamepadKeyCode|GamepadKeyCode The gamepad button which will trigger the prompt. ButtonX

You can connect to proximity prompt events either on the ProximityPrompt object itself or globally through ProximityPromptService. The ProximityPromptService allows you to manage all proximity prompt behavior from one location, preventing any need for duplicate code in your experience.

For more information regarding proximity prompts, see the Proximity Prompts guide.
